summary: Quantify how much a 4-device vs 2-device CXL setup strengthens the FAST/ObjPlace paper, to decide whether to push the DeepTier (ASPLOS) project

synth.extent_4_improves_fast: MODEST and purely QUANTITATIVE — it strengthens evaluation figures but unlocks no new claim class. Mapped to specific claims: (1) The paper's load-bearing NOVELTY — "first real-HW CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference + per-device tail-aware placement/QoS" — is fully established at 2 de-interleaved nodes; 4 adds nothing to it. The decisive never-before-published experiment (victim on CXL-node-A degrading under aggressor on disjoint-core CXL-node-B) needs exactly TWO separate nodes. No prior real-HW paper has this (CXL-Interplay=1 device/testbed, Melody=4 cross-vendor surveyed one-at-a-time with no mitigation, Micron=8 fused into one NUMA node, Weisgut=4 separate-NUMA but placement-only). (2) What 4 STRENGTHENS: turns single data points into curves (1->2->3-aggressor saturation curve, with a possible knee a scheduler can exploit), turns an A-vs-B asymmetry into a device-POPULATION heterogeneity/ranking claim, and turns a binary placement choice into a non-trivial bin-packing search space. (3) The one genuinely DISTINCT claim 4 unlocks — "same-vendor, load-induced device-population heterogeneity + a device-selection QoS scheduler" — is real but second-order, lives in Melody's shadow (reads as "Melody-adjacent + a scheduler," not a second first-of-kind), and is at risk on c28's topology: no CXL switch and all 4 CZ120 share one host bridge, so the most probable 4-device finding is a single shared-upstream bottleneck re-confirmed N times (re-measurement, not new territory), which could collapse the heterogeneity story into "the shared bridge saturates" — itself visible at 2.
what_4_devices_actually_buys: A real saturation curve (victim degradation vs NUMBER of contending devices, 1->2->3 aggressors) instead of a single 1-aggressor data point — hardens the QoS/scheduling justification from assertion to measured mechanism, IF a knee/sub-linear region actually exists on c28's single shared host bridge

A device-POPULATION heterogeneity figure (rank 4 same-vendor CZ120s by tail/bandwidth-under-load; identical at rest, divergent under contention) — the one claim class genuinely unreachable at 2; promotes an A/B anecdote to a distribution/ranking that motivates device-selection QoS over a pool
A non-trivial multi-device bin-packing scheduler search space (vs the degenerate binary choice at 2 devices), enabling a 'beats round-robin/first-fit' result with competing baselines

Easier path to a credible multi-tenant story: real independent tenants co-located on 3+ distinct physical devices, blunting the 'does it compose beyond a pair?' objection more strongly than a 2-device co-tenant

Pre-empts the predictable reviewer objection 'you only had two devices' and matches the nearest competitor's (Weisgut VLDB'25) 4-separate-node testbed scale while delivering the interference+QoS contribution they omitted
what_it_costs: Near-certain schedule slip of DeepTier — a ~5-month, near-complete ASPLOS Sep 2026 submission (~3 months out) that structurally depends on dax0.0/dax1.0 famfs as its CXL storage tier; reclaiming forces it off its substrate mid-crunch

ZERO feasibility de-risking: the hard, unverified firmware gate (root decoders not runtime-programmable; c28 EPYC 9745 = Zen5/Turin with host-bridge decoder port3/decoder3.0 reading locked=1; BIOS interleave-ways=1 knob UNVERIFIED to be exposed and needing admin/BIOS access heavier than the sudo the user already lacks) is IDENTICAL for the 2-node and 4-node paths. 4 does not reduce the hard bet — it only adds DeepTier's cost on top of it

If de-interleave fails, the famfs reclaim yields only 2 MORE 2-way-INTERLEAVED nodes (decoder0.0/0.1 are iw=2) = more device COUNT, not the device GRANULARITY the paper needs — i.e. you pay DeepTier's full cost for the cheap-but-insufficient half of the capability while the per-device payoff stays firmware-blocked

Risk of an active reviewer NEGATIVE: ISCA-style reviewer language de-prioritizes 'raw scale/parameter sweeps' and warns against gains that read as 'from more hardware rather than the mechanism' — a 4-device push framed as scale can invite this critique

Diverts effort from the paper's actual #1 weakness (synthetic aggressor + missing established baselines TPP/MEMTIS/Colloid/SoarAlto), none of which 4 devices fixes — the synthetic-aggressor half is already fixable at 2 nodes with a real co-tenant, and the missing-baselines half is fully orthogonal to device count
synth.minimum_devices_for_a_credible_fast_pape: TWO DE-INTERLEAVED, separately-NUMA-noded CXL devices (not the current fused dax2.0 single node) — achieved by de-interleaving dax2.0 only, leaving DeepTier on dax0.0/dax1.0 famfs. This is the qualitative threshold that crosses from 'characterization' (Melody/Interplay) to 'first device-to-device interference + per-device QoS mitigation on real HW,' and it makes every NEW phenomenon and claim CLASS the paper rests on demonstrable and uncontested. The TRUE go/no-go is not 2-vs-4 — it is whether de-interleave is feasible on c28 AT ALL, which the live-sysfs evidence rates likely-to-fail via software and only maybe via an unverified BIOS knob. Verify that on the 2 system-ram devices you already control before anything else.
synth.the_gate_if_conditional: N/A — recommendation is unconditional (stay 2-device, keep DeepTier). The only contingencies that would tilt toward 4 are both currently false/unverified and the live evidence points against them: (a) a FAST reviewer treating 2 devices as a mere A/B anecdote and demanding a device-population result as an acceptance GATE rather than a strengthening figure (accepted-paper precedent says count is not a gate for mechanism papers), and (b) the BIOS exposing a cheap interleave-ways=1 de-interleave knob that admin grants (live sysfs — root decoders not runtime-programmable, port3 locked=1 on Zen5/Turin — points the other way). Even if both flipped, the right time for 4 is a POST-DeepTier-submission camera-ready robustness pass (after Sep 2026), when its cost collapses to near-zero.
synth.bottom_line: 4 devices improves the FAST paper only MODESTLY and only QUANTITATIVELY — it adds saturation curves, a device-population heterogeneity figure, and a bin-packing scheduler search space, all of which strengthen the evaluation but none of which create a new claim category or move the first-of-kind headline (that headline is fully captured at 2 de-interleaved nodes). It is NOT worth pushing DeepTier. The decisive reasons: (1) the hard firmware de-interleave gate is IDENTICAL for 2 and 4, so 4 buys zero risk reduction and only adds DeepTier's cost; (2) if de-interleave fails, reclaiming famfs yields more INTERLEAVED nodes (count), not the per-device GRANULARITY the paper needs — you would pay the full cost for the insufficient half; (3) accepted top-venue CXL/tiering system papers (Memstrata won while FUSING devices; Colloid/SoarAlto/TPP won on insight with 1-device or pure-emulation testbeds) show device count is never a stated acceptance pillar for mechanism papers; (4) the paper's actual #1 weakness (synthetic aggressor + missing TPP/MEMTIS/Colloid/SoarAlto baselines) is largely orthogonal to device count and is the higher-leverage place to spend effort. Correct sequence: first run a low-cost spike to verify whether c28's BIOS even exposes CXL de-interleave (the true go/no-go); if it works, de-interleave dax2.0 ONLY, keep DeepTier on its famfs devices, ship the cross-device-interference + per-device-placement contribution at 2 separate nodes with a REAL co-located tenant and established baselines, and hold 4-device scaling as an optional post-DeepTier camera-ready robustness pass. Honest uncertainty: this assumes a FAST PC behaves like its OSDI/ASPLOS/SOSP analogs (FAST has fewer public CXL-tiering datapoints), and the whole per-device direction at any device count still hinges on the unverified de-interleave feasibility — verify that before committing to either path.

judges.lens: FAST-reviewer acceptance-odds lens: would 4 devices move a reviewer's score vs 2, given the mechanism is the same?
judges.reasoning:
Through the FAST-reviewer score-delta lens specifically (mechanism held fixed): 4 devices would nudge a reviewer's score, but not across an accept/reject boundary, and the nudge is dominated by lower-cost fixes the paper already owes.

WHAT MOVES A FAST REVIEWER. FAST reviewers reward: (1) a real, non-emulated testbed; (2) a sharp, isolated mechanism; (3) end-to-end wins vs strong baselines; (4) honesty/rigor. Device COUNT is not a stated acceptance pillar for SYSTEM/mechanism papers in any accepted analog (Memstrata OSDI'24 won while FUSING devices into one NUMA node, with a reviewer naming 'multiple devices' as an OPEN QUESTION not a flaw; Colloid/SoarAlto/TPP won on insight with 1-device or pure-emulation testbeds). Device count is a pillar only for CHARACTERIZATION papers (Melody, 4 devices, cross-vendor) — which ObjPlace is NOT. So holding the mechanism fixed, the prior is that count moves a system-paper score weakly.

THE QUALITATIVE THRESHOLD IS AT 2, NOT 4. The single load-bearing novelty experiment — victim on CXL-node-A degrading under aggressor on disjoint-core CXL-node-B — needs exactly TWO separate de-interleaved nodes. That is the experiment no prior real-HW paper has (CXL-Interplay used 1 device/testbed; Melody surveyed devices one-at-a-time and built no mitigation; Micron fused 8). At 2 nodes a reviewer already sees: cross-device interference existence, shared-host-path diagnosis (c28 has NO switch, all 4 CZ120 on one host bridge, so the likely finding is a single shared-upstream bottleneck that 4 devices mostly RE-confirms), per-device tails, the multi-CXL-target placement decision, and cross-device aggregation/QoS. Every NEW phenomenon and claim CLASS the paper rests on is checkable at 2. Going to 4 converts single points into curves (1->2->3 aggressor saturation), an A-vs-B asymmetry into a population/ranking, and a binary placement choice into bin-packing. Real strengthening — a reviewer does like a saturation curve and a heterogeneity figure, and these blunt the predictable 'only two devices / does it compose?' objection — but they raise an already-novel result's polish, not its novelty class. That is precisely a 'reviewer would bump 0.5, not flip a reject to accept' effect.

THE ONE GENUINE SCORE-MOVER, AND WHY IT STILL DOESN'T JUSTIFY THE TRADE. The pro-4 case's strongest point is that 4 nodes let you co-locate REAL independent tenants on distinct physical devices, retiring the paper's own #1 named weakness (the synthetic aggressor). I weight this seriously: per PAPER.md the synthetic aggressor + missing SoarAlto/TPP/Colloid baselines IS the biggest stated risk, and that risk moves scores more than device count does. BUT: (a) the synthetic-aggressor critique is fixable at 2 nodes too — a real second tenant can run on CXL-node-B against a victim on CXL-node-A; you do not need 3-4 devices to make the aggressor 'real,' only to make it a 'population.' (b) The missing established baselines (TPP/MEMTIS/Colloid/hotness) — the other half of the #1 weakness — are completely orthogonal to device count; 4 devices fixes none of them. So the highest-leverage score-mover is reachable without 4, and the part 4 uniquely adds (population heterogeneity) is a Melody-style characterization bonus on top of an already-sufficient systems claim.

THE COST SIDE KILLS IT. The hard, unverified feasibility gate (root decoders are not runtime-programmable; c28's Zen5/Turin fabric decoder reads locked=1; BIOS de-interleave UNVERIFIED to be exposed and needs admin/BIOS access heavier than the sudo the user lacks) is IDENTICAL for 2 and 4 — getting even 2 separate nodes requires the same firmware reprogramming. So 4 buys ZERO feasibility de-risking; it only adds the cost of evicting a near-complete ASPLOS submission (DeepTier, ~3 months out) from its famfs substrate. Worse, the famfs reclaim by itself yields only 2 MORE 2-way-INTERLEAVED nodes (decoder0.0/0.1 are iw=2), i.e. device COUNT not device GRANULARITY — you would pay DeepTier's full cost for the cheap-but-insufficient half of the capability while the granularity you actually need stays firmware-blocked regardless. And ISCA'25-style reviewer language actively de-prioritizes 'raw scale/parameter sweeps' and warns against gains that look like they come 'from more hardware rather than the mechanism' — so a 4-device push could even invite a mild negative read if framed as scale.

VERDICT THROUGH THIS LENS: 4 vs 2 is a MODEST positive on a FAST reviewer's score (it adds curves, a heterogeneity figure, and an easier path to a multi-tenant story — worth perhaps a fractional bump and some objection-proofing), but it is not decisive: it neither creates a new claim class nor fixes the baseline gap that actually gates acceptance, and the score-moving part (real co-tenant) is largely reachable at 2. Given that the cost is pushing a near-done ASPLOS submission for a capability whose hard gate is shared with the 2-device path and whose extra yield is the wrong (interleaved, not per-device) kind, it is NOT worth pushing DeepTier. Recommended sequence: (1) verify BIOS de-interleave on the 2 system-ram devices first — the true go/no-go; (2) ship the cross-device-interference + device-granular-placement contribution at 2 separate nodes with a REAL co-located tenant and TPP/Colloid/hotness baselines; (3) hold 4-device saturation/heterogeneity curves as an optional camera-ready robustness pass IF de-interleave proves feasible AND DeepTier has submitted.

judges.lens: Novelty/competitive-freshness: does 4-device cross-interference occupy meaningfully more open territory than 2-device, given CXL-Interplay=1, Micron=8-fused, Melody=4-cross-vendor, Weisgut=4-separate-NUMA-but-placement-only?
judges.reasoning: Through the freshness lens, the competitive boundary in the verified literature sits at ">=2 co-located, de-interleaved, mutually-contending real CXL devices," NOT at 4. The proof is in the competitors' own device counts: Micron used EIGHT devices yet bought zero interference-freshness because fusion erased per-device granularity (so raw count is demonstrably not the freshness currency); Weisgut PUBLISHED 4 separately-NUMA-noded devices and still did not claim interference/QoS (so a 4-separate-node config is already-published infrastructure, not fresh territory by itself); CXL-Interplay at 1 device cannot do CXL-to-CXL at all. The paper's PRIMARY open territory — "first real-HW CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference + per-device tail-aware QoS mitigation" — is therefore fully captured at 2 de-interleaved nodes. Going to 4 does relocate the boundary on exactly ONE secondary axis: load-induced SAME-VENDOR device-population heterogeneity (identical-at-rest, divergent-under-load) plus device-selection QoS over a pool, which is a distribution/ranking claim that genuinely needs N>=3-4. That axis is open (Melody did heterogeneity but CROSS-VENDOR and built NO mitigation), so 4 devices upgrades the paper from "first cross-device interference" to additionally "first same-vendor load-induced population QoS." That is a real but SECOND-ORDER freshness gain, and it lives in Melody's shadow — a reviewer reads it as "Melody-adjacent, strengthened with a scheduler," not as a second first-of-kind. Two facts cap it at modest rather than substantial: (1) the first-of-kind HEADLINE does not move from 2 to 4; (2) c28 has no switch and all 4 CZ120 share one host bridge, so the most probable 4-device result is the same shared-upstream bottleneck re-confirmed N times — re-measurement, not new territory — putting the heterogeneity story itself at risk of collapsing into "the shared bridge saturates," a 2-device finding. Worth-pushing verdict: NO. The only freshness 4 adds is a second-order, Melody-shadowed, c28-topology-at-risk increment that does not relocate the paper's primary novelty boundary (already crossed at 2). Because the hard firmware de-interleave gate (Zen5/Turin root decoders not runtime-programmable, port3 locked=1) must clear identically for 2 and 4, the freshness-bearing 4-device config is not even de-risked relative to 2 — pushing a near-complete ASPLOS submission to buy a second-order freshness increment fails the freshness-lens cost/benefit.

judges.lens: Research-portfolio cost/risk: marginal FAST gain vs. concrete cost of pushing a near-complete ASPLOS project + de-interleave feasibility risk
judges.reasoning:
Through the cost/risk lens, the trade is asymmetric and net-negative. Decompose into the three levers the portfolio actually faces.

1) MARGINAL FAST GAIN FROM 4 vs 2 (modest, not decisive). The convergent verdict across analyses is that every NEW phenomenon and claim CLASS the FAST novelty rests on — first real-HW CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference, shared-host-path contention diagnosis, per-device tail latency, multi-CXL-target placement, cross-device aggregation/QoS — is fully demonstrable at 2 de-interleaved nodes. What 4 adds is uniformly QUANTITATIVE: 1->2->3-aggressor saturation curves, A/B-asymmetry promoted to a population ranking, binary placement promoted to bin-packing. These are real strengthening figures (reviewers like a 4-device asymmetry plot and a degradation-vs-N curve), but accepted-paper evidence shows device count is never a stated acceptance pillar for SYSTEM/mechanism papers (Memstrata won while FUSING devices; Colloid/SoarAlto/TPP won on insight with 1-device or pure-emulation testbeds). Device count is a pillar only for CHARACTERIZATION papers (Melody). So I rate the gain modest — above negligible because the heterogeneity-population and saturation-curve stories are genuinely unreachable at 2 and do harden the QoS-mechanism justification, but well short of decisive because they create no new claim category and risk the ISCA-style 'gains from hardware not mechanism' critique.

2) THE FEASIBILITY GATE IS SHARED — and this is the pro-4 camp's best point, but it cuts the other way on cost/risk. Both 2-separate-nodes and 4-nodes require the same firmware/root-decoder de-interleave (root decoders not runtime-programmable; c28 EPYC 9745 = Zen5/Turin with port3/decoder3.0 locked=1). The live-sysfs evidence rates this gate as LIKELY-TO-FAIL via software and only maybe achievable via an UNVERIFIED BIOS knob requiring admin/BIOS access on a shared HPC node (heavier than the sudo the user already lacks), possibly impossible for the same-host-bridge mem2/mem3 pair. So the shared gate means 4 buys ZERO feasibility de-risking — it does not reduce the hard bet, it only adds the incremental famfs-reclaim cost. And critically, reclaiming famfs WITHOUT de-interleave yields only 2 more 2-way-INTERLEAVED nodes (decoder0.0/0.1 are iw=2) = device COUNT, not the device GRANULARITY the paper needs. You would pay DeepTier's full cost for the cheap-but-insufficient half of the capability.

3) OPPORTUNITY COST (the lens's core). DeepTier is ~5 months in, near-complete, ASPLOS Sep 2026 (~3 months out), and structurally depends on dax0/dax1 famfs. Reclaiming those forces it off its substrate mid-crunch with near-certain slip — a concrete, high-probability loss of a near-done submission. Against that, the ObjPlace gain is (a) low-probability for the part that matters (per-device granularity, firmware-blocked) and (b) merely strengthening even if it lands. Expected-value: you are trading a high-certainty, near-term, near-complete paper for a low-probability hardware capability whose payoff over the 2-device config is only quantitative. That is a poor portfolio bet.

ORDERING OF RISK. The decision question ('is 4 worth pushing DeepTier') is premature: the binding constraint is whether de-interleave works on 2 devices AT ALL, which is unverified and evidence-weighted toward no. Correct sequencing: (i) low-cost spike to confirm whether c28's BIOS exposes CXL interleave-ways=1 and admin will set it; (ii) prove de-interleave on the 2 system-ram devices already controlled — no DeepTier impact; (iii) ship the cross-device-interference + per-device-placement contribution on 2; (iv) the highest-leverage remaining weakness per the paper's own docs is the SYNTHETIC aggressor / missing real two-tenant workload and absent SOTA baselines (TPP/MEMTIS/Colloid/SoarAlto) — none of which 4 devices fixes, and which deserve the effort instead. Hold 4-device scaling as an optional camera-ready robustness pass IF de-interleave proves feasible AND DeepTier has submitted (post-Sep-2026), when its cost collapses to near-zero.

CAVEAT honoring the pro-4 case: if a reviewer treats 2 devices as 'just an A/B anecdote' and demands a device-population result as a GATE, or if a BIOS knob turns out cheaply available, the calculus tilts toward 4. But the live evidence points against cheap de-interleave, and accepted-paper precedent says count is not a gate for mechanism papers — so neither contingency justifies pushing a near-complete submission NOW.

VERDICT: 4-vs-2 value is modest; not worth pushing DeepTier. Take 2 (de-interleave dax2.0 only), keep DeepTier on its famfs devices, spend marginal effort on de-interleave verification and the real-tenant/baseline gaps, and defer 4 to a post-DeepTier camera-ready pass.

cases.position: Going to 4 devices (de-interleaving dax2.0 AND reclaiming dax0.0/dax1.0 from famfs, pushing DeepTier) materially strengthens the FAST paper along the SAME firmware-feasibility risk envelope as the 2-device minimum, and is worth it BECAUSE the 4-device configuration is what converts ObjPlace from a single-phenomenon demonstration into a quantitative, generalizable systems contribution that directly retires the paper's two named weaknesses (synthetic aggressor, single-device) — provided BIOS de-interleave proves feasible at all (the same hard gate either path must clear).
strongest_points: THE FEASIBILITY GATE IS SHARED, SO 4 DEVICES IS NEARLY 'FREE' RISK: The feasibility analysis is explicit that getting even 2 SEPARATE CXL NUMA nodes requires the exact same root-only/BIOS decoder de-interleave as the 4-device path — root decoders are not runtime-programmable and the Turin/Zen5 fabric decoder reads locked=1, blocking BOTH the 2-node and 4-node software paths identically. This collapses the core counter-argument: the hard, unverified gate (decoder reprogramming on CZ120/Turin) is paid in full just to reach the >=2-node go/no-go minimum. Conditional on that gate clearing, the ONLY incremental cost of 4 over 2 is the cheap, reversible, root-only famfs reclaim (umount + daxctl reconfigure, minutes-scale). You are already betting the paper on the firmware bet; 4 devices does not add a second hard bet, it adds curves on top of the same bet.

4 DEVICES IS THE LEVER THAT RETIRES THE PAPER'S OWN #1 WEAKNESS (SYNTHETIC AGGRESSOR). The reviewer-value analysis and PAPER.md both name the synthetic aggressor + missing real two-tenant workload as the biggest actual weakness — and the multi-device literature analysis states explicitly that going to 4 devices 'makes the synthetic-aggressor critique easier to retire by enabling real co-located tenants on distinct devices.' With 4 de-interleaved nodes (DRAM + 3 CXL targets, or victim + multiple aggressor devices) you can co-locate genuinely independent real tenants on distinct physical devices instead of a synthetic stream aggressor sharing the fabric. This is the single highest-leverage fix the docs ask for, and device-granularity at N>=3-4 is what makes a multi-tenant-on-distinct-devices story credible rather than an A-vs-B anecdote.

4 DEVICES UNLOCKS A DISTINCT CLAIM CLASS THAT 2 CANNOT: DEVICE-POPULATION HETEROGENEITY. The experiment-delta analysis concedes that 'real CXL devices form a heterogeneous population with load-induced per-device asymmetry in tail latency, motivating device-selection QoS over a pool' NEEDS N>=3-4 to be a population claim rather than an A/B anecdote. This is precisely the axis Melody (ASPLOS'25, 4 devices) made its entire reputation on — but Melody did it CROSS-VENDOR and built NO mitigation. ObjPlace at 4 SAME-VENDOR CZ120 devices can show load-INDUCED asymmetry (devices identical at rest, divergent under contention) AND build the per-device QoS mitigation Melody explicitly left as future work. That combination — population-scale heterogeneity + a working device-selection scheduler — is a headline neither Melody nor any prior paper holds, and it is unreachable at 2.

2 DEVICES YIELDS ONLY A SINGLE DATA POINT WHERE REVIEWERS EXPECT A CURVE — AND THE CURVE IS THE WHOLE QoS ARGUMENT. The experiment-delta analysis states that with 2 devices you get exactly ONE 1-aggressor data point and 'cannot show whether a shared host resource saturates linearly, sub-linearly, or has a knee.' For a QoS/scheduling contribution this is load-bearing, not cosmetic: a per-device admission/placement scheduler is only justified if victim degradation as a function of the NUMBER of contending devices is non-trivial (has a knee or sub-linear region a scheduler can exploit). The 1->2->3 aggressor saturation curve, the bin-packing search space (degenerate/binary at 2 devices per the analysis), and the aggregation-plateau curve all turn ObjPlace's 'device-as-schedulable-resource' framing from an assertion into a measured, defended mechanism — which is exactly the 'isolated mechanism win' the ISCA'25 reviewer notes reward.

THE CLOSEST COMPETITOR (Weisgut VLDB'25) ALREADY PROVES 4 SEPARATELY-NUMA-NODED DEVICES IS PUBLISHABLE INFRASTRUCTURE — SO 4 IS A CREDIBILITY FLOOR, NOT A STRETCH. The literature analysis notes Weisgut configured 4 CXL devices as separate NUMA nodes but stopped at data-placement/bandwidth and never claimed cross-device interference or per-device QoS. Matching their 4-device testbed while delivering the interference + QoS contribution they omitted directly out-positions the nearest neighbor on its own hardware scale, pre-empts the predictable 'you only had two devices / does this compose beyond a pair?' reviewer objection, and demonstrates generality (the analysis lists 'does a per-device QoS/placement policy still hold with 4 contenders' as a real generality question 2 cannot answer).
cases.key_risk_if_this_position_is_wrong: The entire case is conditional on a firmware bet that the feasibility evidence rates as likely-to-FAIL: root decoders are not runtime-programmable, c28's Turin/Zen5 fabric decoder reads locked=1, and BIOS de-interleave is UNVERIFIED to even be exposed (production BIOSes often hardcode interleave policy), requires BIOS access on a shared HPC node heavier than the sudo the user already lacks, and may be physically impossible for the same-host-bridge mem2/mem3 pair regardless. If de-interleave fails, the famfs reclaim buys only MORE interleaved nodes (device count, not device granularity) — the per-device contribution dies AND DeepTier was pushed for nothing: a strictly negative outcome. Secondarily, even if feasible, the c28 has no CXL switch and all 4 CZ120 share one host bridge, so the most probable finding is a single shared-upstream bottleneck already visible at 2 devices, making the 4-device curves re-confirmations rather than new phenomena — and the accepted-paper evidence (Memstrata won while FUSING devices; Colloid/SoarAlto/TPP won on insight with 1-device or emulated testbeds) shows device count is never a stated acceptance pillar for system papers, so the marginal acceptance gain may not cover the cost of slipping a near-complete ASPLOS submission. The mitigation that keeps this position honest: do NOT push DeepTier until a low-cost spike PROVES BIOS de-interleave works on 2 devices first; reclaim the famfs devices only after the hard gate is confirmed cleared.

cases.position: 2 de-interleaved CXL NUMA nodes are SUFFICIENT for a strong FAST paper, and pushing DeepTier to obtain 4 devices is a poor trade. The 2-vs-4 question is the wrong axis: every NEW phenomenon and claim category the paper's novelty rests on is fully demonstrable at 2 separate CXL nodes, while 4 devices only adds quantitative reinforcement of claims already made. The genuine go/no-go risk is the de-interleave feasibility gate (firmware-locked on Turin/Zen5), which is IDENTICAL for 2 and 4 — so 4 does not de-risk the paper, it only adds DeepTier's cost. Take 2 (de-interleave dax2.0 only), keep DeepTier on dax0/dax1 famfs, and hold 4-device scaling as an optional camera-ready robustness pass.
strongest_points: The single load-bearing novelty experiment needs exactly 2 nodes. The defensible FAST contribution (deep-research Idea 1) is 'first real-HW CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference + per-device tail-aware placement/QoS.' The decisive, never-before-published experiment — victim on CXL-node-A degrading (or not) under aggressor on disjoint-core CXL-node-B — requires exactly TWO separate CXL NUMA nodes. No prior real-HW paper has this: CXL-Interplay (DAC'25, the self-described 'first real-HW CXL interference') used ONE device per testbed and only studied CXL-vs-DRAM and CXL-vs-SSD; Melody (ASPLOS'25) has 4 devices but surveys them one-at-a-time cross-VENDOR and explicitly builds NO mitigation; the Micron 8-device Xeon-6 study FUSED all 8 into one NUMA node. The cross-device co-location axis is untouched and is unlocked at 2.

Every distinct PHENOMENON the contribution rests on is demonstrable at 2 nodes; 4 only adds quantity. With 2 de-interleaved nodes you can show: cross-device interference existence, shared-host-path contention diagnosis (c28 has NO CXL switch and all 4 CZ120 share one host bridge, so the likely finding is a single shared upstream bottleneck — already visible at 2), per-device tail latency and whether one device's tail is perturbed by load on the other, the multi-CXL-target placement mechanism (DRAM vs CXL-A vs CXL-B), cross-device bandwidth aggregation vs shared-path cap, and per-device QoS by steering a tenant onto the alternative device. Live c28 sysfs shows the fused system-ram node is produced by root decoder0.2 with interleave_ways=2; kernel docs state root decoders are 'not runtime programmable,' and c28's EPYC 9745 is exactly the Zen5/Turin platform the docs flag for 'pre-program and lock HDM decoders' (host-bridge decoder port3/decoder3.0 reads locked=1). Getting even 2 separate nodes requires the same root-decoder/firmware reconfiguration as getting 4. Therefore 4 adds zero feasibility margin; it only adds the extra step of reclaiming famfs. And reclaiming famfs alone yields 2 MORE 2-way-INTERLEAVED nodes (decoder0.0/0.1 are iw=2) — more device COUNT, not the device GRANULARITY the paper needs. You would pay DeepTier's full cost for the cheap-but-insufficient half of the capability.

Accepted top-venue CXL/tiering papers win on mechanism + real-HW + end-to-end wins, NOT device count. Memstrata (OSDI'24) won while FUSING CXL into one tiered NUMA node, and a reviewer explicitly listed 'how multiple CXL devices affect performance' as an open QUESTION, not a reject reason. Colloid (SOSP'24) won on one insight, SoarAlto (OSDI'25) on a single ASIC CXL device, and TPP (ASPLOS'23, now in Linux) on pure NUMA emulation with ZERO real devices. Device count is a stated pillar only for CHARACTERIZATION papers (Melody) where cross-device variance IS the finding — not for a system/mechanism paper like ObjPlace. ISCA'25 reviewer notes actively de-prioritize 'raw scale/parameter sweeps' and reward isolated mechanism wins, and warn against gains that come 'from hardware rather than the mechanism' — a risk a '4 devices = more headroom' result invites.

ObjPlace already clears the acceptance pillars at the single-node level; the gating asset is the qualitative jump to >=2 separate nodes, which 2 supplies. Measured on real HW (repo RESULTS.md): bandwidth-bound CXL victim 2.0-2.13x slowdown under co-tenant, latency-bound <=1.23x, DRAM ~none; ObjPlace matches manual oracle within <1%, beats Linux interleave ~14.3% on skewed embedding gather, beats hotness-only +118% in the sensitivity case, ~0.2% steady overhead. These hit the real-HW, sharp-mechanism, and beats-strong-baselines pillars. The remaining weakness is qualitative (cross-device interference is currently only single-node + SYNTHETIC aggressor), and that is closed by 2 de-interleaved nodes — not by adding devices 3 and 4.

Opportunity cost is asymmetric and negative. DeepTier is ~5 months in, near-complete, ASPLOS Sep 2026 (~3 months out), and depends on dax0/dax1 famfs as its CXL storage tier. Reclaiming those devices forces it off its substrate mid-crunch with near-certain slip. In exchange ObjPlace gains, with high certainty, only 2 more INTERLEAVED nodes; the per-device granularity that is the paper's whole point stays firmware-blocked regardless of count. Trading a near-done submission for the cheap-but-insufficient half of a low-probability capability is poor expected value. Higher-leverage effort: verify de-interleave feasibility on the 2 system-ram devices already controlled, and retire the synthetic-aggressor critique with a real co-located tenant — neither of which 4 devices addresses.
cases.key_risk_if_this_position_is_wrong: The position fails if a FAST reviewer treats 2 devices as 'just an A/B anecdote' and demands a device-population result (asymmetry ranking, N-contender saturation curve) as an acceptance gate rather than a strengthening figure — in which case the heterogeneity/scaling story that genuinely needs N>=3-4 becomes load-bearing and 2 is insufficient. A second, compounding risk: if de-interleave is actually feasible on c28 cheaply (e.g., a BIOS interleave-ways=1 knob is exposed and admin grants it), then the marginal cost of going to 4 drops sharply and the DeepTier-vs-4 trade tilts back toward 4 — but this remains UNVERIFIED and the live-sysfs evidence (root decoders not runtime-programmable, port3 locked=1 on Zen5/Turin) points the other way, so even 2 is not yet proven achievable. The honest precondition for the entire position is verifying de-interleave on 2 before committing.

experiments_possible_with_2dev: Existence of CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference: victim on CXL-node-A, aggressor on CXL-node-B (disjoint cores), measure whether A's bandwidth/latency degrades. This is the single decisive novelty experiment (no prior real-HW work has it; CXL-Interplay DAC'25 used 1 device). Qualitatively shown with exactly 2 separate CXL NUMA nodes.

Path-sharing diagnosis: determine whether two CZ120s contend through a shared upstream (host CXL bridge / PCIe root complex / CPU memory controller) or are isolated. 2 devices answer the yes/no that the whole contribution hinges on.
Per-device vs cross-device interference contrast: same-device co-tenant (2.0-2.13x, already measured) vs cross-device co-tenant. 2 devices give the A-vs-B comparison.
Per-device tail-latency existence and a 2-way device-to-device tail comparison (Melody-style us p99.999), including whether one device's tail is perturbed by load on the other.
'Which CXL device' placement decision: the planner routing an object to DRAM vs CXL-A vs CXL-B (one alternative target). The multi-CXL-target placement mechanism EXISTS at 2 nodes.

2-device bandwidth aggregation point: stripe one bandwidth-bound object across 2 CXL nodes and test whether you get ~2x35.5 GiB/s or hit a shared-path cap. The key qualitative 'does aggregation help or is it capped' question is answered with 2.

Per-device QoS / placement-arbitration mechanism: protect a victim by steering/admitting a tenant onto the alternative device. The mechanism is demonstrable with a victim device + 1 alternative = 2 devices.
Cross-device R/W-mix steering: route reads to one device and writes to another, or rebalance under a co-tenant, exploiting bidirectional PCIe. Demonstrable at 2.
INTERLEAVE planner candidate validated across real CXL nodes (fixes the GNN-uniform -11.6% loss) using 2 CXL nodes + DRAM.

experiments_needing_4dev.experiment: Aggregate cross-device pressure saturation curve: sweep 1 -> 2 -> 3 aggressor devices against one victim device and plot how victim degradation grows with the NUMBER of contending devices. A real CURVE (vs a single point) needs >=3 aggressors, i.e. 4 total.
experiments_needing_4dev.why_needs_3_or_4: With 2 devices you get one (1-aggressor) data point; you cannot show whether a shared host resource saturates linearly, sub-linearly, or has a knee. The shape of the saturation is a genuinely new quantity only visible at 3-4.

experiments_needing_4dev.experiment: Contention asymmetry / heterogeneity across a device population: rank 4 devices by tail and bandwidth-under-load and show they are NOT interchangeable (load-induced per-device asymmetry), justifying 'which specific device' QoS decisions over a population.
experiments_needing_4dev.why_needs_3_or_4: Asymmetry as a distribution/ranking needs N>=3-4 to be more than an A-vs-B anecdote; 2 devices can show a difference but not that device selection over a pool is a real scheduling problem.

experiments_needing_4dev.experiment: Bandwidth aggregation plateau / scaling shape: stripe across 1,2,3,4 devices and locate where aggregate BW plateaus against the shared upstream cap.
experiments_needing_4dev.why_needs_3_or_4: The plateau point and curve shape need >2 stripe widths; 2 devices give only the first segment.

experiments_needing_4dev.experiment: Multi-device bin-packing QoS scheduler at scale: arbitrate several tenants across 4 devices (combinatorial placement) and show the scheduler beats naive round-robin / first-fit.
experiments_needing_4dev.why_needs_3_or_4: The packing problem is degenerate with 2 devices (one binary choice); a scheduling contribution with a non-trivial search space and competing baselines is more convincing at 4.

experiments_needing_4dev.experiment: N-1-on-1 pathological pattern (all other devices' traffic funneled to starve one victim via the shared path).
experiments_needing_4dev.why_needs_3_or_4: Maximal cross-device pressure on a single victim is only reachable with multiple aggressor devices; quantifies worst-case isolation failure.

headline_claims_only_4_unlocks: 'Victim degradation scales with the number of contending CXL devices' (the saturation curve) - a quantitative claim, not a new phenomenon.

'Real CXL devices form a heterogeneous population with load-induced per-device asymmetry in tail latency, motivating device-selection QoS over a pool' - needs N>=3-4 to be a population claim rather than an A/B anecdote.
'Our scheduler solves the multi-device placement/bin-packing problem' as a scaling result with a non-trivial search space and competing schedulers.
Aggregate-bandwidth scaling/plateau shape across a device array.
gather.does_interference_qualitatively_change_2: No. The QUALITATIVE core - that CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference exists (or that devices are isolated), that contention flows through a shared host path (no switch on c28, all 4 CZ120 on one host bridge), that per-device tails exist and can be perturbed cross-device, and that the placement engine must make a 'which CXL target' decision and can arbitrate/aggregate across CXL nodes - is fully established with 2 SEPARATE CXL NUMA nodes. The single decisive 'is there cross-device interference at all' experiment that grounds the entire Idea-1 contribution (and that no prior real-HW paper has) needs only 2. Going to 4 changes interference QUANTITATIVELY: it turns single data points into curves (1->2->3 aggressors), turns an A-vs-B asymmetry into a population/ranking, and turns a binary placement choice into a bin-packing problem. These strengthen the evaluation but do not create a new phenomenon or a new claim category - they are bigger versions of the 2-device result. Important caveat: '2 devices' here must mean 2 DE-INTERLEAVED separate CXL NUMA nodes, not the current fused dax2.0 single node; getting 2 separate nodes already requires the same root-only decoder reprogramming as the 4-device path, so the hard feasibility gate (de-interleave on CZ120/Turin) is identical for 2 and 4 - 4 only additionally costs reclaiming famfs from DeepTier.
gather.reasoning: Grounding in the repo (docs/PAPER.md, docs/RESULTS.md, docs/DESIGN_OBJPLACE.md, DEEP_RESEARCH_2026-06-12.html): the FAST paper's defensible novelty (deep-research Idea 1) is 'first real-HW CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference + per-device tail-aware placement/QoS.' The load-bearing, never-before-shown experiment is simply victim-on-device-A degrading (or not) under aggressor-on-device-B - that needs exactly TWO separate CXL NUMA nodes. Every distinct PHENOMENON the contribution rests on (cross-device interference existence, shared-host-path contention, per-device tails, multi-CXL-target placement, cross-device aggregation/QoS) is demonstrable at 2. What 4 devices add is uniformly QUANTITATIVE: saturation curves (1->2->3 aggressors), a device-population asymmetry/heterogeneity story, a non-trivial bin-packing scheduler search space, and aggregation-plateau curves. These are real strengthening factors for a top-venue evaluation - reviewers like a 4-device asymmetry figure and a 'degradation grows with N contenders' curve - but none is a headline that unlocks acceptance; they make existing claims more convincing rather than enabling a new claim. Three facts cap the marginal value at SMALL: (1) c28 has NO CXL switch and all 4 CZ120 share one host bridge, so the most likely finding is a single shared-upstream bottleneck whose existence is already visible at 2 devices - more devices mostly re-confirm the same bottleneck. (2) The hard, unverified feasibility gate (root-only decoder de-interleave on CZ120/Turin) is identical for the 2-separate-node and 4-node configs; 4 does not de-risk the paper, it only adds the cost of evicting DeepTier from famfs. (3) The paper's biggest actual weakness per its own docs is the SYNTHETIC aggressor and missing established baselines (TPP/MEMTIS/Colloid/SoarAlto) and no real two-tenant workload - none of which 4 devices fixes; researcher effort is better spent there. Recommendation implied by the analysis: take 2 separate CXL NUMA nodes (de-interleave dax2.0 only), keep DeepTier on dax0/dax1 famfs, ship the cross-device-interference + device-granular-placement contribution, and add 4-device curves later as a camera-ready/strengthening pass IF de-interleave proves feasible and DeepTier has submitted. Pushing DeepTier now to grab 4 devices buys mostly bigger figures, not a stronger central claim.

findings.claim: Melody (Systematic CXL Memory Characterization and Performance Analysis at Scale, ASPLOS'25, Virginia Tech) uses 4 real CXL Type-3 memory expanders, but they are 4 DIFFERENT-VENDOR devices (CXL-A/B/C/D) characterized largely one-at-a-time per platform. 'Cross-device' in Melody means cross-vendor comparison of per-device latency/bandwidth/tail behavior (per-device average latency 214-394ns; one-NUMA-hop latency increases of 161ns/202ns/227ns/94ns; some devices show us-level p99.999 tail latency at low utilization). Contention experiments co-locate CPU pointer-chase/traffic threads against ONE CXL device, NOT two CXL devices against each other. Melody explicitly does NOT build mitigation (frames tail latency + QoS as future work; offers Spa, a diagnosis tool, not a runtime).
findings.device_count_relevance: Device count IS load-bearing to Melody's contribution (the 'not all CXL are created equal' / cross-vendor variability message needs >=4 devices), but the devices are surveyed independently, not co-run. This is the strongest evidence that per-device CXL tail latency is real AND that nobody has built device-to-device interference characterization or per-device QoS mitigation on top of it. It is the single best citation for 'the gap ObjPlace/Idea-1 fills is open.' Going 1->4 here bought a cross-VENDOR survey; it did NOT buy cross-device co-location, which is exactly the untouched axis.

findings.claim: CXL-Interplay (DAC'25) / CXL-Interference (arXiv:2411.18308, same authors/content; Tsinghua, ICT-CAS, Alibaba, Zhejiang) uses exactly ONE CXL device per system: System A = Montage ASIC-based CXL expander + SAS SSD; System B = Intel FPGA-based CXL expander + NVMe SSD. It characterizes interference between (1) main memory (MMEM) and CXL and (2) neighboring storage (NVMe/SAS SSD) and CXL. It NEVER studies CXL-to-CXL (device-to-device) interference because each testbed has only one CXL device.
findings.device_count_relevance: Device count is NOT load-bearing in the multi-device sense; it is the canonical 'first real-HW CXL interference' paper but on a single device, with the interference axis being CXL-vs-DRAM and CXL-vs-storage. Directly supports the claim that cross-CXL-device interference is unpublished. Confirms the project's prior understanding exactly.

findings.claim: The Micron/Intel study (Optimizing System Memory Bandwidth with Micron CXL Memory Expansion Modules on Intel Xeon 6, arXiv:2412.12491) uses EIGHT Micron CZ122 128GB CXL E3.S devices on one Xeon 6 6900P host, but explicitly FUSES all 8 into ONE unified NUMA node via software weighted page-interleaving (Linux 6.11.6). It reports only aggregate bandwidth gains (+24% read-only, +39% mixed R/W; 24% geomean speedup) and optimal DRAM:CXL interleave weights. No per-device analysis, no cross-device interference, no per-device QoS/tail latency.
findings.device_count_relevance: Highest device count found (8) but device count is load-bearing ONLY for aggregate bandwidth; the per-device dimension is deliberately erased by fusion into one NUMA node. This is the strongest evidence that even with 8 devices the field has not done device-granular analysis, which validates ObjPlace's de-interleaved per-device angle as novel. It is also a near-twin of c28's current dax2.0 fused config, so it is a direct 'what NOT to claim if you stay fused' reference.

findings.claim: Weisgut et al. (CXL Memory Performance for In-Memory Data Processing, PVLDB Vol.18 No.9, 2025, HPI) uses FOUR CXL memory devices on one host (Emerald Rapids), AND configures each device as a SEPARATE NUMA node, interleaving data across up to 4 devices. But its contribution is in-memory-DB data-placement strategies (column placement by access frequency) and aggregate bandwidth scaling; its 'contention' analysis is CPU memory-controller contention, not CXL-to-CXL device interference. No per-device QoS or per-device tail-latency study.
findings.device_count_relevance: This is the closest match to BOTH 'multiple real devices as separate NUMA nodes' AND ObjPlace's placement-by-access-pattern angle, so it is the most important competitor to distinguish from. Crucially it shows that even a 4-device, separately-NUMA-noded, placement-oriented paper did NOT claim cross-device interference or per-device QoS, leaving that contribution open. Device count is load-bearing for its bandwidth-aggregation claims but NOT used for any device-granular isolation/QoS result.

findings.claim: A related VLDB result (cited in search) reports round-robin page interleaving across 2/3/4 CXL devices yielding 1.9x/2.3x/2.5x throughput vs one device for sequential 4KiB reads. This is pure bandwidth aggregation across fused/interleaved devices, not per-device or interference work.
findings.device_count_relevance: Quantifies what going 1->2->4 devices buys IF you fuse them: monotonic but sub-linear bandwidth aggregation. Relevant because it sets the bar for the ONLY thing extra devices straightforwardly buy when pooled (bandwidth), as opposed to the device-granular contribution ObjPlace would claim.

findings.claim: Demystifying CXL Memory with Genuine CXL-Ready Systems and Devices (MICRO'23, UIUC, arXiv:2303.15375) accommodates only ONE physical CXL device; the authors explicitly note 'our system can accommodate only one CXL memory device' and that future platforms 'may connect up to four CXL memory devices.' Foundational real-HW characterization, single device.
findings.device_count_relevance: Device count NOT load-bearing (single device). Confirms that the foundational real-CXL characterization paper anticipated 4-device platforms but could not study them, again leaving the multi-device-on-one-host axis open. Also the source of the 'NUMA emulation is misleading' framing the project relies on.

findings.claim: Exploring and Evaluating Real-world CXL (UC Merced, arXiv:2503.17864) uses a SINGLE 128GB CXL device (system A) and proposes a data-object-level interleaving policy (beating Linux page interleaving by ~65%) for CXL+DRAM tiering. Object-level placement angle overlaps conceptually with ObjPlace, but on one device with no per-device interference/QoS.
findings.device_count_relevance: Single device; device count not load-bearing. Important as a positioning neighbor because it independently validates 'object-level placement > page interleaving' (supports ObjPlace's beats-interleave claim) while leaving the multi-device/device-granular contribution untouched.

findings.claim: Equilibria (Fair Multi-Tenant CXL Memory Tiering At Scale, Meta) does fair multi-tenant CXL tiering on REAL production hardware (explicitly argues against emulation), mitigating noisy-neighbor interference and meeting SLOs. But it operates at the page-migration/tiering policy level treating CXL as a single tier; it does NOT partition or schedule per physical CXL device. This is the device-side analog to the MTTM/Equilibria 'DRAM-tier partitioning' competitors the project already identified.
findings.device_count_relevance: Device count not the axis; CXL treated as one tier. Confirms that even the most production-grade multi-tenant CXL QoS work is tier-level, not per-device, so per-device CXL QoS remains unclaimed. This is the main competitor to differentiate from on the 'QoS' part of Idea 1.

findings.claim: Cloud-native DB CXL works that DO use multiple devices across hosts (PolarCXLMem/Alibaba-XConn, Oasis-SOSP'25, Octopus, 'My CXL Pool Obviates Your PCIe Switch') rely on a CXL SWITCH for cross-host memory pooling/sharing. They are out of scope for c28 (no switch, single host) and study pooling/disaggregation, not single-host per-device interference or QoS.
findings.device_count_relevance: Multiple devices but switch-based and pooling-focused; not applicable to c28's switchless single-host config and not the device-granular interference axis. Useful only to scope ObjPlace explicitly AWAY from switch/pooling claims and to note the single-host de-interleaved niche is uncrowded.

gather.bottom_line:
Across all recent (2023-2026) real-hardware CXL papers I could verify against primary PDFs, NO ONE has published cross-CXL-device (device-to-device) interference OR per-device QoS on >=2 real CXL devices co-located on one host. The multi-device papers split cleanly into two camps: (a) FUSE devices into one NUMA pool and report only aggregate bandwidth (Micron 8-device Xeon-6 study; the 2/3/4-device 1.9x/2.3x/2.5x interleave-scaling result), or (b) treat devices as separate NUMA nodes but for data-placement/bandwidth, never for interference or QoS (Weisgut VLDB'25, 4 devices, separate NUMA nodes, in-memory-DB column placement). The interference/QoS papers are all single-device or single-tier: CXL-Interplay/CXL-Interference (1 device, CXL-vs-DRAM and CXL-vs-SSD only), Melody (4 devices but cross-VENDOR survey, threads-vs-one-device contention, explicitly no mitigation), Demystifying-CXL and Merced (1 device), Equilibria (tier-level multi-tenant QoS, CXL as one tier). The project's prior understanding of the gap is correct and well-supported.

On the load-bearing question (1->2 vs 2->4): Going from 1 to 2 real, SEPARATELY-NUMA-NODED CXL devices is the qualitative threshold — it is the minimum that lets you make the genuinely-new claims (cross-device interference, per-device tail/QoS, device-as-schedulable-resource) that literally no prior paper makes; it crosses from 'characterization' (Melody/Interplay did this) to 'first device-to-device interference + per-device QoS mitigation on real HW.' Going from 2 to 4 is quantitative reinforcement, not a new claim class: it strengthens generality (does cross-device interference compose/scale beyond a pair? does a per-device QoS/placement policy still hold with 4 contenders?), makes the synthetic-aggressor critique easier to retire by enabling real co-located tenants on distinct devices, and pre-empts a reviewer 'only-two-devices' objection — but Weisgut already shows 4 separately-noded devices is publishable infrastructure, and the FAST novelty is fully unlocked at 2. 

Recommendation implication: the >=2 separately-NUMA-noded-CXL go/no-go is the real bar and it alone makes the core FAST contributions claimable and uncontested. 4 devices is a robustness/generality multiplier with diminishing marginal novelty, so it is hard to justify pushing a near-complete ASPLOS submission (DeepTier) to obtain it. The higher-leverage gap to close first is not device COUNT but the synthetic-vs-real-tenant critique (Melody/Interplay are pure characterization; nobody co-runs real tenants on distinct devices) and de-interleave FEASIBILITY on CZ120/Turin, which is still UNVERIFIED and is the actual precondition for any per-device claim at any count. Verify de-interleave on 2 devices before considering reclaiming 4.

findings.claim: Memstrata / Intel Flat Memory Mode (OSDI'24), a top accepted CXL paper, won on MECHANISM + WORKLOAD-SCALE, not device count. Its strength was page-coloring to kill inter-VM contention + an online slowdown estimator, validated on a real CXL prototype against ~115 DIMM-class configs and Azure-scale traces (188 workloads / >100,000 VMs). Critically, its hardware-tiered mode INTERLEAVES CXL memory across multiple CXL devices at cache-line granularity *within one NUMA node* - i.e., the paper did NOT do device-granular NUMA, and still won.
findings.device_count_relevance: Directly on-point: a top venue accepted a CXL paper that fused devices into one tiered NUMA node (the same fused-NUMA situation as c28's dax2.0). Per-device separation was not required for acceptance. The reviewer blog explicitly listed 'how multiple CXL devices would affect performance' as an unexplored open QUESTION, not a reject reason - i.e., 4-vs-2 is a 'nice future direction,' not an acceptance gate.

findings.claim: Colloid (SOSP'24, 'Tiered Memory Management: Access Latency is the Key!') was accepted on a single counter-intuitive INSIGHT - place pages to balance *loaded* access latency across tiers (DRAM latency rises under load and can exceed CXL), not hotness - and demonstrated it by retrofitting HeMem/TPP/MEMTIS. The contribution is the principle + mechanism, not testbed scale.
findings.device_count_relevance: Shows the dominant acceptance factor at a top OS venue is a sharp mechanism/insight that reframes the problem. A small-device real-HW (or even mixed) testbed is sufficient when the idea is strong. ObjPlace's analogue (bandwidth-sensitivity/skew/phase placement) is the load-bearing asset, not 2-vs-4 devices.

findings.claim: TPP (ASPLOS'23), the canonical CXL tiering baseline now upstreamed into the Linux kernel, was evaluated on NUMA-EMULATED CXL (dual-socket, CPU-less remote NUMA node mimicking CXL), not a real CXL device at all. It won on a transparent OS page-placement mechanism (+10-17% over NUMA balancing/AutoTiering, 44x faster reclaim) plus Meta fleet workload characterization.
findings.device_count_relevance: Counterexample bounding the 'real hardware' axis: the most influential tiering mechanism paper used ZERO real CXL devices. This means real-hardware-at-all is valued but is not strictly mandatory if the mechanism and workload story are strong - and it makes clear that going from 2 to 4 real devices is far down the priority list versus the mechanism + end-to-end win.

findings.claim: SoarAlto / AOL (OSDI'25, 'Tiered Memory Management Beyond Hotness') was accepted on a new METRIC (amortized offcore latency capturing latency x MLP) and two mechanisms (SOAR profile-guided allocation, ALTO migration regulation), evaluated on a single ASIC-based 128GB CXL expander (one device) on Sapphire Rapids.
findings.device_count_relevance: Another 2025 top-venue accept with effectively ONE real CXL device. Confirms that beyond having a real device, the differentiator is the insight/metric and integration breadth (TPP/NBT/Nomad/Colloid), not device count. ObjPlace adding a 2nd-vs-4th device buys little reviewer credit here.

findings.claim: Melody (ASPLOS'25) is the heavyweight that DOES use 4 real CXL devices - but its 4-device scope buys it CHARACTERIZATION breadth (265 workloads, 7 latency levels, 5 CPU platforms, first disclosure of CXL tail latencies; 3 of 4 devices show unstable high tails). It is explicitly a measurement/characterization study and does NOT build a mitigation system.
findings.device_count_relevance: This is the key nuance: multi-device scale pays off for a CHARACTERIZATION paper (where cross-device variance IS the finding). For a SYSTEM/mechanism paper like ObjPlace, the device count is justification for the problem, not the contribution. ObjPlace can cite Melody's 4-device variance to motivate per-device QoS without needing 4 of its own. 2 de-interleaved devices already let you SHOW CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference (the unfilled gap) - the qualitative result (>1 device, real, de-interleaved) is what's missing in the field, not 4-vs-2.

findings.claim: CXL-Interplay (DAC'25), the self-described 'first real-HW CXL interference' work, used two separate systems each with ONE CXL device (one Montage ASIC, one Intel FPGA) and characterized interference between CXL and other memory/storage - NOT CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference. The cross-device-interference + per-device QoS space is genuinely open.
findings.device_count_relevance: Confirms the differentiating gap is QUALITATIVE (>=2 real CXL devices, de-interleaved, studied against each other), which 2 system-ram devices already satisfy. The novelty is 'CXL-to-CXL exists and is schedulable,' provable with 2 devices; 4 devices is incremental scale on top of an already-novel result.

findings.claim: Real CXL hardware is measurably and qualitatively different from NUMA emulation (Demystifying CXL, ASPLOS'25-adjacent / Melody: up to ~26% latency and 3-66% bandwidth error; +27ns idle, +37ns loaded; emulation misses microsecond tail latencies entirely). Multiple reviews treat real-HW measurement as the gold standard over simulation.
findings.device_count_relevance: The high-value axis is real-hardware-AT-ALL (which both 2- and 4-device configs satisfy) plus capturing real-CXL-only phenomena (us tails, loaded latency, cross-device interference). Crossing from emulation to real is the big reviewer credit; 2->4 devices does not move on this axis.

findings.claim: Real ISCA'25 reviewer language (a memory/architecture venue) prioritizes: validation rigor ('without validation every performance number is speculative'), ISOLATED non-confounded contributions ('reject when gains are dominated by hardware assumptions rather than the novelty of the mechanism'), and non-obvious insight over parameter sweeps. No reviewer language premiumizes raw device count / scale.
findings.device_count_relevance: Reviewers explicitly devalue 'raw scale' and explicitly reward isolated mechanism wins and rigor. Adding 2 more devices is closer to a 'scale/parameter sweep' than to a new isolated contribution - low marginal reviewer value, and risks the 'gains from hardware not mechanism' critique if the win is just 'more devices = more headroom.'

findings.claim: Across all sampled accepted tiering/CXL system papers (Memstrata, Colloid, SoarAlto, TPP, Nomad-OSDI'24), the recurring acceptance pillars are: (1) a real-CXL or credible testbed, (2) a sharp mechanism/insight, (3) END-TO-END application wins vs strong SOTA baselines (TPP, MEMTIS, hotness, Linux interleave), and (4) integration breadth / generality. Device COUNT never appears as a stated pillar for system papers.
findings.device_count_relevance: ObjPlace's current results already hit pillars 1-3 (real HW; bandwidth-sensitivity placement insight; beats Linux interleave ~14%, hotness-only +118%, matches oracle <1%, ~0% overhead). The marginal FAST acceptance gain from 4-vs-2 devices is small relative to the cost; the gating need is the QUALITATIVE de-interleave (>=2 separate CXL NUMA nodes) to demonstrate real CXL-to-CXL interference + per-device QoS - which 2 devices supply.

gather.bottom_line: Evidence from accepted 2023-2026 CXL/tiering papers at OSDI/ASPLOS/SOSP/FAST-adjacent venues strongly indicates that, for a SYSTEM/mechanism paper like ObjPlace, reviewer assessment is dominated by (b) the mechanism/insight, (c) having REAL hardware at all (vs emulation), and (d) end-to-end workload wins vs strong baselines - NOT by (a) raw device count. Concretely: Memstrata (OSDI'24) won while FUSING CXL devices into one tiered NUMA node and a reviewer treated 'multiple devices' as an open question, not a flaw; Colloid (SOSP'24) and SoarAlto (OSDI'25) won on a single insight/metric with one-device-class testbeds; TPP (ASPLOS'23), the canonical baseline now in Linux, used pure NUMA emulation. The ONE place device count pays off is CHARACTERIZATION papers (Melody, ASPLOS'25, 4 devices) where cross-device variance is itself the finding. For ObjPlace, the decisive, non-substitutable asset is the QUALITATIVE jump to >=2 DE-INTERLEAVED real CXL NUMA nodes so you can demonstrate genuine CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference and per-device QoS - the verified open gap (CXL-Interplay used 1 device/system and never did CXL-to-CXL; Melody characterized but built no mitigation). That gap is provable with 2 de-interleaved devices. Going from 2 to 4 is incremental 'more scale/headroom,' which ISCA'25 reviewer notes actively de-prioritize versus isolated mechanism contributions, and risks the 'gains come from hardware not the mechanism' critique. NET RECOMMENDATION FOR THE DECISION: 4 devices does NOT materially change FAST acceptance odds once you have >1 real de-interleaved device; it is not worth pushing DeepTier (a near-complete ASPLOS submission) off its famfs devices. The real go/no-go risk is not 2-vs-4 - it is whether the 2 fused dax2.0 devices can be DE-INTERLEAVED into 2 separate per-device NUMA nodes at all (root CXL-decoder reprogramming, UNVERIFIED on CZ120/Turin). Spend the effort verifying de-interleave feasibility on the 2 system-ram devices you already control; if that works, you have a FAST-strength testbed without touching DeepTier's devices. Keep 4-device scale as an optional 'extends to N devices' robustness section, not a prerequisite. Caveats: this is inference from accepted-paper testbeds, public reviewer blogs, and one architecture-venue review set - FAST's specific PC has fewer public CXL-tiering datapoints than ASPLOS/OSDI, so the strongest direct analogues are memory-venue papers; and PDF text extraction failed for two sources so exact Memstrata/Colloid device-count integers are taken from secondary summaries, though the qualitative testbed claims are corroborated across multiple sources.

findings.claim: Root decoders are NOT runtime-reprogrammable, and this is the gate for de-interleaving. The Linux CXL driver doc states root decoders are 'a logical construct' that is 'not runtime programmable'; only switch/endpoint decoders can be user-programmed 'if the platform supports such configurations.' On c28 the system-ram node (NUMA node 1 / dax2.0, 512 GiB) is produced by root decoder0.2 with interleave_ways=2, granularity=256B. You cannot change a root decoder's interleave_ways from 2 to 1 at runtime; the 2-way fusion is baked into the BIOS-published CFMWS window. De-interleaving via 'cxl/daxctl region+decoder reconfiguration' as the task hypothesizes is therefore blocked at the root-decoder level, independent of any teardown.
findings.device_count_relevance: This is the core blocker for splitting the 1 fused 512 GiB system-ram node into 2 per-device nodes. If the root decoder cannot be reprogrammed, software-only de-interleave (the cheap path) is not available on this box.
findings.source: Live sysfs on c28: decoder0.2 interleave_ways=2 ig=256 target_list='0,0' locked=0; kernel doc https://docs.kernel.org/driver-api/cxl/linux/cxl-driver.html ('Root Decoders ... not runtime programmable')

findings.claim: c28 is hit by the documented AMD Zen5/Turin 'pre-program-and-lock HDM decoders' quirk. The EPYC 9745 is Zen5/Turin. The kernel doc explicitly names this: 'Some platforms may require pre-programming HDM decoders and locking them due to quirks (see: Zen5 address translation), but this is not the normal, expected configuration path,' and 'Auto Decoders ... are almost always locked (cannot be changed).' On c28 the host-bridge port decoder port3/decoder3.0 reads locked=1. So even below the root decoder, the fabric decoder for the system-ram pair is locked by firmware. 'Platforms requiring boot-time programming and/or locking of CXL fabric components may prevent features, such as device hot-plug, from working' — i.e. the dynamic reconfiguration this project needs is the exact class of feature firmware-locking disables.
findings.device_count_relevance: Confirms the de-interleave is not merely unsupported by tooling but actively firmware-locked on this specific silicon. Strong evidence that splitting dax2.0 into 2 per-device NUMA nodes is infeasible without a BIOS/firmware change (admin + vendor BIOS options), not just root commands.
findings.source: Live sysfs on c28: /sys/bus/cxl/devices/port3/decoder3.0 locked=1; kernel docs https://docs.kernel.org/driver-api/cxl/linux/cxl-driver.html and https://docs.kernel.org/driver-api/cxl/platform/bios-and-efi.html

findings.claim: The actual c28 topology differs from the project-context assumption and makes the per-device goal harder. There are 4 CZ120 endpoints across 3 BIOS-created CFMWS windows: decoder0.0 (242 GiB, iw=2, targets host bridges e0+c0 = mem0+mem1) and decoder0.1 (269 GiB, iw=2, same e0+c0 pair) are the famfs devdax devices (dax0.0 + dax1.0); decoder0.2 (512 GiB, iw=2, targets host bridge pci0000:00 twice = mem2+mem3 = endpoint5/endpoint6) is the system-ram node 1 (dax2.0). So the 'fused' system-ram pair sits behind ONE host bridge (port3), while the famfs pair is interleaved across TWO host bridges (e0 and c0). Both pairings are 2-way BIOS interleaves. Note only mem2/mem3 currently enumerate as cxl memdevs with full endpoint decoders; the e0/c0 devices are represented at root-decoder level. Getting 4 independent per-device NUMA nodes requires de-interleaving BOTH a same-host-bridge pair (mem2/mem3, the locked/Zen5 case) AND a cross-host-bridge pair (mem0/mem1) — two distinct firmware reconfigurations, both root-decoder-level.
findings.device_count_relevance: Going from the current 1 system-ram node to 2 per-device nodes needs the locked same-host-bridge split; going to 4 needs that PLUS reclaiming+de-interleaving the famfs cross-bridge pair. The 4-node target is strictly the union of two hard firmware reconfigurations, not one.
findings.source: Live sysfs on c28: cxl list -BMPv, daxctl list -DR, decoder target_list values; mount shows /dev/dax0.0 and /dev/dax1.0 as famfs fuse mounts

findings.claim: The realistic path to per-device CXL NUMA nodes is a BIOS/firmware change, not a runtime root command. Because root decoders aren't runtime programmable and the Turin fabric decoder is locked, splitting interleave requires changing how firmware publishes CFMWS windows — i.e. a BIOS setup-menu change to set CXL interleave ways to 1 (one window per host bridge) and/or disable cross-device interleave, then reboot. This is gated on: (a) the AMI/AMD BIOS on c28 actually exposing such a knob (UNVERIFIED — many production BIOSes hardcode the pooling/interleave policy), (b) admin/root access to enter BIOS on an ARC cluster node (the user has no passwordless sudo as of 2026-04-18, and BIOS access on a shared HPC node is a heavier ask than sudo), (c) the change surviving cluster reprovisioning. Even if granted, the same-host-bridge pair (mem2/mem3) may not be separable at all if firmware always interleaves the two ports of one host bridge.
findings.device_count_relevance: Determines effort/owner: this is an admin+BIOS+reboot+vendor-docs task with an unknown success bit, not a 30-minute daxctl session. Effort is high and the outcome is genuinely uncertain (could be impossible for the mem2/mem3 pair specifically).
findings.source: Synthesis of kernel CXL docs (root decoder not runtime programmable; Zen5 lock quirk; boot-time locking disables reconfig features) + c28 sysfs state + CLAUDE.md note that ghu4 has no passwordless sudo

findings.claim: Reclaiming dax0.0/dax1.0 from famfs is the EASY, low-risk part — but it only yields 2 MORE interleaved nodes, not 2 per-device nodes, unless the same firmware de-interleave succeeds. Software-wise: umount the two famfs fuse mounts, daxctl reconfigure-device --mode=system-ram --no-online dax0.0 dax1.0, daxctl online-memory. That is a minutes-scale, reversible, root-only operation. BUT decoder0.0 and decoder0.1 are each iw=2 root decoders, so onlining them as system-ram gives you 2 additional 2-way-interleaved nodes (242 GiB and 269 GiB), still NOT per-device. Per-device separation of mem0/mem1 again requires the same firmware/root-decoder reprogramming that is blocked at runtime. So 'reclaim famfs' buys you device-COUNT of system-ram nodes but not device-GRANULARITY.
findings.device_count_relevance: Clarifies that the device-count lever (more NUMA nodes) is cheap, but the device-granularity lever (the thing Idea-1 actually needs for CXL-to-CXL cross-device interference) is the expensive/blocked one. Reclaiming famfs alone does NOT unlock per-device QoS work.
findings.source: Live c28 mounts (famfs fuse on dax0.0/dax1.0) + decoder0.0/0.1 interleave_ways=2 in sysfs; CLAUDE.md daxctl reconfigure procedure

findings.claim: Opportunity cost of pushing DeepTier is high and asymmetric against an uncertain ObjPlace gain. DeepTier is ~5 months in, near-complete, targeting ASPLOS Sep 2026 (next ~3 months), and depends on dax0.0/dax1.0 famfs as its CXL storage tier. Reclaiming those devices forces DeepTier off its substrate during its submission crunch, with near-certain schedule slip. The ObjPlace side gains at most 2 extra INTERLEAVED system-ram nodes from that reclaim (high certainty), but the actually-paper-relevant per-device granularity gain is blocked by the Zen5 lock / non-runtime-programmable root decoders (so the 4-separate-node payoff is low-probability on this exact hardware). Trading a near-term, near-done ASPLOS submission for a low-probability hardware capability is a poor expected-value bet.
findings.device_count_relevance: Directly answers 'is 4 worth pushing DeepTier': the reclaim is cheap and certain to yield more nodes, but those nodes are interleaved, and the de-interleave needed to make them per-device (the FAST paper's whole point) is the part that is firmware-blocked. So you would pay the full DeepTier cost for the cheap-but-not-sufficient half of the capability.
findings.source: Project context (DeepTier status/dependency) + c28 firmware/decoder findings above

gather.bottom_line: FEASIBILITY: De-interleaving the fused 512 GiB system-ram node (dax2.0/NUMA node 1) into 2 per-device nodes via cxl/daxctl is NOT achievable at runtime on c28. Live sysfs shows it is produced by root decoder0.2 with interleave_ways=2, and root decoders are not runtime-reprogrammable (kernel doc); worse, c28 is an AMD EPYC 9745 = Zen5/Turin, which the kernel doc explicitly flags as a platform that 'pre-programs HDM decoders and locks them' — and indeed the host-bridge decoder port3/decoder3.0 reads locked=1. So the cheap software path is blocked. The only realistic route to per-device granularity is a BIOS/firmware change (set CXL interleave ways to 1 / disable cross-device interleave, reboot), which is UNVERIFIED to even be exposed on this BIOS, requires admin + BIOS access on a shared HPC node (heavier than the sudo the user already lacks), and may be impossible for the mem2/mem3 same-host-bridge pair regardless. EFFORT/RISK: high effort, admin-and-vendor-gated, with a genuine chance it is simply impossible on this silicon — not a daxctl afternoon. Reclaiming dax0.0/dax1.0 from famfs IS cheap, reversible, and root-only, BUT it only yields 2 MORE 2-way-INTERLEAVED system-ram nodes (decoder0.0/0.1 are iw=2), not 2 per-device nodes — it raises device COUNT, not device GRANULARITY, which is the thing the FAST/Idea-1 direction actually needs. OPPORTUNITY COST: pushing DeepTier (near-done, ASPLOS Sep 2026, dependent on those famfs devices) to gain at most extra interleaved nodes — while the per-device capability stays firmware-blocked — is a bad expected-value trade. RECOMMENDATION: Do NOT push DeepTier for this. First spend a low-cost spike confirming whether c28's BIOS exposes a CXL interleave-ways=1 option and whether admin will set it; only if that de-interleave is proven possible does going to 4 (or even 2) per-device nodes become real. Absent that, the honest hardware ceiling is multiple interleaved system-ram nodes, and the paper's per-device-resource framing should be re-scoped to what 1-2 reconfigurable-but-interleaved CXL nodes can actually demonstrate, or moved to hardware where root/fabric decoders are user-programmable.
